A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FAST/FAST-GRPO research. All 16 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including appendices, tables, equations and figures, support comparison. Renamed and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original Geometry3K pilot experiments, seven-benchmark evaluations, component ablations, sampling comparisons and sensitivity analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds human evaluation, statistical reporting, method variants, 32B-model experiments, cross-domain evaluations and failure analyses.

M1.justification: v2 adds continuous Slow-to-Fast sampling, with easy-sample probability increasing to 0.4, alongside the retained binary schedule. It also tests weighted-sum difficulty instead of multiplication (Appendices H–I). These are limited procedural variants; the default conditional length reward and adaptive KL rule remain.

E1.justification: The original training sources and seven main benchmarks remain. v2 substantially broadens evaluation through MM-K12 science reasoning, Bingo and MMHal open-domain VQA/hallucination evaluation, MMVP visual perception, and MMEval-Pro calibrated multimodal evaluation (Appendix K).

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 adds an early-stopped naive-GRPO comparator absent from v1 Table 6. The main slow-thinking comparator set in Table 3 and Kimi, CosFn and DAST in Table 4 remain unchanged. The additional scaling and cross-domain comparisons principally use already represented method families.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 32B configuration trained for three epochs, whereas v1 evaluates 3B/7B models with ten-epoch training. New evaluation designs include three participants rating 200 images on a five-point scale, a 1,000-sample difficulty diagnostic, and validation-based early stopping around step 150. These extend the experimental design rather than replace the retained main protocol.

E4.justification: v2 adds human validation of image complexity, naive-GRPO overfitting diagnostics, multiplicative-versus-weighted-sum and binary-versus-continuous comparisons, and systematic failure categorization with new examples. The original sampling, SFT and hyperparameter analyses remain; converting the latter into Figure 4 is a presentation change.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run uncertainty reporting. v2 Appendix G adds standard deviations across five runs at temperature 0.1, error bars and p<0.05 significance markings for the main benchmark results. This newly documents uncertainty; it does not establish an increase in training runs. The significance test and training-seed procedure remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Table 3 and Table 4's existing per-benchmark scores are unchanged. v2 adds human correlations, early-stopped GRPO results, formulation/scheduling variants, 32B results and cross-domain scores. For example, Table 15 newly reports FAST-7B/base MM-K12 accuracy of 62.2/53.6 and response lengths of 371.2/477.6. Those lengths imply 22.3% shortening, contradicting the text's 33.8% claim.

T1.justification: The written image-complexity definition changes from averaged H(v_i) terms to H(v), explicitly defined over class probabilities (v1 Equation 4; v2 Equation 2). v2 also restores the KL coefficient beta in Equation 1 and defines the weighted-sum score and continuous schedule. The existing gradient argument remains, without new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the core contribution: adapting reasoning through question characteristics, length rewards and difficulty-aware KL regularization. The headline seven-benchmark claim, over 10% relative accuracy improvement and 32.7–67.3% token reduction remain. Emphasizing FAST-GRPO rather than FAST does not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets naive-GRPO behavior as overfitting, discusses misleading multiplicative difficulty scores and reward safeguards, and attributes remaining failures primarily to visual perception. It also explains the continuous curriculum's accuracy–length tradeoff and explicitly limits demonstrated scaling to 32B models. These substantially extend v1's interpretations and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds GLCM quantization and patch-size details, human-rating instructions, scheduling parameters and 32B compute information. Most existing hyperparameters are relocated unchanged. It omits the explicit 180K intermediate preprocessing count and introduces an H20 hardware statement while retaining the 600 H100 GPU-hours description, leaving resource reporting inconsistent.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Tree-of-Mixed-Thought, Visual Agents as Fast and Slow Thinkers, PPO, the added benchmarks and amplified multimodal hallucination. Some earlier citations are removed. The main positioning against slow-thinking LVLMs and length-control methods for LLMs remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites and reorganizes the narrative: GRPO background and pilot experiments become separate sections, related work moves after experiments, and implementation details and existing case studies move into appendices. Difficulty terminology is recast, and the title and author list change. This exceeds simple expansion with new scientific content.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a predominantly single-column layout with wrapped displays. v1 Tables 9–11 become the three-panel v2 Figure 4, the original case figure moves to Appendix L, and new diagnostic, uncertainty and failure figures are added. Table 4 gains averages, alongside several new experimental tables.

improvement.justification: v2 improves assessability through broader domain/scale evaluation, human validation, an early-stopped GRPO comparison and uncertainty reporting. However, new reporting problems limit the gain: Table 12 shows a 1.5-point MathVision difference despite the text claiming differences within 0.5, and Table 15 supports 22.3% rather than 33.8% shortening against the base model. The unspecified significance test further limits the statistical claims. The added evidence is useful, but its integration and interpretation remain insufficiently checked.
